::: {.why}
The oldest systematic strategy in the business, and looking at it as a filter rather than as folklore tells you exactly what it is betting on and where it stops working.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Express a moving-average crossover as a linear filter on past returns and say what shape of autocorrelation it profits from.
- Say what a trend follower's return distribution looks like relative to a normal, and which option position it resembles.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Do the algebra: write the position of a fast-minus-slow moving average crossover as a weighted sum of past returns, and plot the weight profile. It is a band-pass filter, and the shape tells you which frequencies of autocorrelation it is long.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Measure the payoff shape: plot your 12-month momentum rule's monthly return against the index's monthly return as a scatter, and fit a quadratic. The convexity you find is the thing practitioners mean when they say trend following is long volatility.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
A trend follower loses money in a market that oscillates and makes money in one that moves. State that as a property of the autocorrelation function it needs.
